To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
absent or reversed end-diastolic velocity in umbilical artery is a strong predictor of neonatal death in preterm neonates.
AREDF is a predictor of adverse outcome in preterm neonates.
AREDF was independently predictive of neonatal mortality and major morbidity, but was not associated with long-term neurodevelopmental outcome.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the association of antenatal Doppler flow with neonatal outcome.
the prediction of adverse neonatal outcomes in preterm neonates.
the use of the Doppler ultrasound technique to study the blood flow in the umbilical arteries of pregnant women.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the presence of AREDF is an early predictor of mortality and morbidity in VLBW neonate.

the absence of a diastolic flow in the umbilical artery in a very preterm fetus is associated with an increased risk for mortality and morbidity, and that this risk is independent of other confounding factors.
AREDF is an early predictor of mortality in VLBW (AGA) neonates.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
AREDF is an important predictor of mortality in VLBW neonate.
the absence/reversal of end diastolic flow in umbilical artery (AREDF) is associated with increased risk for mortality and major neonatal morbidity.
AREDF was an independent predictor for mortality in the NICUs of our study.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the presence of AREDF should be considered an important risk factor for mortality in the NICUs in developing country settings.

the use of umbilical artery doppler in the antenatal period can identify high-risk pregnancies and may help in the planning of appropriate management strategies to reduce neonatal mortality and morbidity in VLBW neonate.
the presence of AREDF should not be considered a benign finding.
